title: Tunable Memory Effect in Dissipative Strongly Correlated Quantum Systems
authors: Haowei Li, Yu Chen, Hui Zhai
abstract: Strongly interacting quantum many-body systems subjected to non-Markovian dissipation pose a formidable challenge due to the interplay between strong correlation effects and memory effects. In this Letter, we develop a general theoretical framework to compute how a system observable responds to dissipation, which captures memory effects at short times and recovers the Markovian limit at longer times. Using this framework, we predict that, for a strongly correlated quantum critical state with critical exponent $η$, the short-time dynamics of a system observable always obeys a $t^{2η}$ scaling law. This emerges as a universal result from the interplay between strong correlation and memory effects, independent of the microscopic Hamiltonian of the system. We further reveal a crossover behavior of this scaling law to either $t^{2η-1}$ or linear-in-$t$ behavior beyond the memory time scale. We propose a concrete physical realization of a non-Markovian bath with tunable memory time using ultracold atoms, where our predictions can be straightforwardly verified in current experiments.
summary: This work develops a general theory to describe how observables evolve in strongly correlated quantum systems coupled to non-Markovian baths. It predicts that the initial time evolution is governed by a universal $t^{2\eta}$ scaling law, which then smoothly transitions into longer-time Markovian behavior. The framework is applicable to ultracold atomic gas simulations.
main_problem: The study addresses how strongly correlated quantum many-body systems behave when subjected to non-Markovian dissipation, capturing the interplay between strong correlations and memory effects.
main_result: The short-time dynamics of a system observable in a critical state universally follows a $t^{2\eta}$ scaling law, which then crosses over to either $t^{2\eta-1}$ or linear-in-$t$ behavior at longer times.
method: The authors develop a general theoretical framework using linear response theory and perturbative expansions in the coupling strength ($J$) to calculate observable changes ($\delta W(t)$).
model_or_system: The analysis uses general models of strongly interacting particles coupled to an environment, with specific examples including two-mode Bose systems and one-dimensional interacting Bose gases (Lieb–Liniger Hamiltonian).
key_observables: Change in observable ($\delta W(t)$), total atom number ($\hat{N}$), momentum occupation ($\hat{n}_k$), and spectral densities ($S^{(1)}, S^{(2)}$).
important_parameters: Critical exponent $\eta$, memory time $t_0 = 1/\Gamma$, dissipation time $t_d$, and the coupling strength $J$.
main_assumptions: The theory relies on perturbative expansions, a factorized two-frequency spectral density approximation, and assuming applicability of edge power laws over low-energy frequency windows.
figures_summary: Figures compare full master equation simulations against response theory predictions for conserved and nonconserved observables in Bose systems, illustrating the crossover from short-time quadratic/power-law growth to linear-in-$t$ behavior.
paper_structure: The paper establishes a general theoretical framework for dissipation response, derives scaling laws for both conserved and nonconserved observables across different time regimes ($t \ll t_0$, $t_0 \ll t \ll t_d$), and applies these results to specific quantum gas models.
why_interesting: The universal prediction of the $t^{2\eta}$ scaling law for short-time dynamics, independent of microscopic details, provides a powerful diagnostic tool for characterizing memory effects in strongly correlated quantum gases.
